messages.content: I want to investigate whether language models can revise temporal inferences when a narrative is corrected, without treating an underspecified event order as settled.

That is the central question: can a model update the temporal judgments that a correction affects while preserving uncertainty wherever the narrative still does not determine the order of events? A correction should not prompt either indiscriminate revision or an unsupported choice of order.
What counts as a temporal judgment here?

It is a judgment about a temporal claim relative to the narrative. The three classifications in the goal are entailed, contradicted, and undetermined. Entailed means the narrative supports the claim; contradicted means it supports an incompatible temporal conclusion; undetermined means the available information does not settle the claim either way.
So undetermined is not just another way to say contradicted?

Right. If a narrative leaves open whether one event preceded another, a claim that it did precede it is not thereby contradicted. It is undetermined. Keeping that distinction is essential to preserving uncertainty about underspecified event order.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming anything about the narratives we would use?

As an abstract illustration, suppose a description says nothing that fixes the order of event A and event B. The claim “A happened before B” would remain undetermined on that information. If a corrected description establishes that B happened before A, that same claim would instead be contradicted. The illustration shows how a correction can change a judgment; it does not specify any particular task narrative.
And if the correction establishes A before B?

Then, in that abstract illustration, “A happened before B” would be entailed. The classification follows the information available in the corrected narrative. If the corrected narrative still leaves their order open, the appropriate classification remains undetermined.
Does revising an inference mean reconsidering every temporal claim?

A model may need to consider what the correction implies, but the goal is not to change every judgment. It calls for updating judgments affected by narrative corrections while preserving previously correct judgments that are unaffected. Whether a claim is affected depends on whether the correction changes what the narrative supports about that claim, including implications for its event order.
I want the preservation condition stated precisely.

The requirement is to preserve at least 95% of previously correct temporal judgments unaffected by narrative corrections, while updating affected judgments. The 95% threshold concerns that previously correct, unaffected set; it is not a requirement to keep judgments that a correction renders inappropriate.
Does that percentage tell us how many affected judgments must be updated?

No separate numerical threshold for updating affected judgments is stated. Updating them is part of the requirement, but the ≥95% figure specifically quantifies preservation of previously correct judgments that the corrections do not affect. The two parts should not be collapsed into one percentage.
How do the three classifications fit into the performance goal?

The stated performance target is macro-F1 ≥0.85 when classifying temporal claims as entailed, contradicted, or undetermined on unseen event structures. Macro-F1 gives each of those three classes equal weight in its average, so the target is about classification across the full set of labels, not just recognizing claims with a specified order.
Does macro-F1 ≥0.85 require an F1 of at least 0.85 for each label?

Not by itself. The stated threshold applies to macro-F1, the average across the classes; it does not state a separate ≥0.85 threshold for entailed, contradicted, and undetermined individually. It also should not be read as an achieved score—the value is a requirement for the investigation.
Why specify unseen event structures?

The goal is for the classification performance to hold on event structures the model has not already encountered in the relevant evaluation context, rather than being limited to familiar structures. The node does not prescribe particular structures or a way to construct them; “unseen event structures” states the condition under which the macro-F1 target applies.
Could a model meet the classification target yet still mishandle corrections?

The two requirements address different aspects of the goal. Macro-F1 ≥0.85 concerns classifying temporal claims on unseen event structures. The ≥95% preservation requirement, together with updating affected judgments, concerns how judgments behave when a narrative is corrected. Neither requirement should be treated as a substitute for the other.
I'm especially concerned about a model becoming overconfident whenever it sees a correction.

That concern is consistent with the goal. A correction may resolve some temporal relationships while leaving others underspecified. The model should revise inferences that the correction changes, but it should continue to mark a temporal claim undetermined when neither the correction nor the rest of the narrative establishes or rules out that claim.
Could a correction turn an entailed claim into an undetermined one, rather than its opposite?

Conceptually, yes. If a corrected narrative no longer fixes an order that had supported the claim, and does not establish the opposite order either, the claim could become undetermined. A correction need not turn every affected claim directly from entailed to contradicted or vice versa. The appropriate label depends on what the corrected narrative actually determines.
What if a correction mentions one event but changes a conclusion about other events indirectly?

The relevant distinction is whether the temporal judgment is affected, not merely whether the claim repeats words from the correction. If changing one ordering also changes what follows about another ordering, that other judgment can be affected. Conversely, a previously correct judgment remains in the preservation set only if the correction leaves it unaffected.
So preservation is not just copying the model's earlier answers?

Exactly. Copying earlier answers indiscriminately would fail to update affected judgments. The ≥95% requirement concerns retaining previously correct judgments that remain unaffected, while the goal also calls for revision where the corrected narrative changes the warranted inference. Preserving uncertainty matters as well: an earlier undetermined judgment should not become a definite one without sufficient information.
And this is an investigation, not a claim that language models already meet those thresholds?

Yes. The node sets out what to investigate and the required outcomes: macro-F1 ≥0.85 for the three-way classification on unseen event structures, and preservation of ≥95% of previously correct, unaffected temporal judgments while updating affected ones. It does not report a completed experiment or establish that either threshold has been met.
Let me check the core distinction one last time: a corrected narrative can warrant a new temporal conclusion, but it does not license guesses about every remaining event order.

That's the distinction. The model should follow the corrected narrative where it changes what is entailed or contradicted, keep previously correct judgments that it leaves unaffected, and use undetermined for claims whose event order remains underspecified.
How could we approach the goal without having the model reconsider every temporal claim from scratch after a narrative correction?

One proposal is to have an LLM extract temporal constraints from the narrative, tag those constraints with their provenance, incrementally recompute the affected closure when a correction arrives, and classify claims by bidirectional reachability. The idea is to make explicit which ordering information supports an inference and which inferences may need revision when that information changes.
What does a provenance-tagged temporal constraint mean here?

A temporal constraint expresses an ordering supported by the narrative. Its provenance identifies where that constraint came from, so it can be associated with the relevant narrative information rather than treated as an unsupported fact. If a correction changes that information, the tag helps identify a constraint whose contribution to later inferences needs reconsideration. The proposal does not specify a particular tag format.
Is the LLM meant to produce the final entailed, contradicted, or undetermined label directly?

In this proposal, the LLM's stated role is to extract provenance-tagged temporal constraints. The proposed classification step then uses bidirectional reachability over the resulting temporal information. That separates what the narrative says about ordering from the determination of whether a queried temporal claim follows, is opposed, or remains unresolved.
Can you unpack “closure” without assuming a particular implementation?

Closure refers to temporal consequences that follow from the extracted constraints, including consequences that are not stated directly. For example, if the constraints establish that A precedes B and B precedes C, then A precedes C is a consequence. Recomputing the affected closure means reconsidering the consequences that may change after a correction, rather than treating all previously derived consequences as equally affected.
Why call the recomputation incremental?

Because the proposal focuses on updating what the correction affects in the existing set of constraints and their consequences. It is not a claim that the entire set of temporal judgments must be discarded and inferred anew after every correction. Nor does “incremental” itself specify a particular procedure or guarantee a performance improvement.
How would provenance matter for an inference that uses several constraints?

It matters because a derived ordering can depend on information from more than one part of the narrative. In the abstract A-before-B, B-before-C illustration, a conclusion that A precedes C relies on the constraints establishing both links. If a correction changes a supporting link, that derived conclusion is among those to reconsider. Provenance is intended to help connect the conclusion to the information that supports it; the proposal does not prescribe an exact representation for those dependencies.
What is bidirectional reachability in this setting?

For a claim that A precedes B, one checks whether the temporal constraints support a path from A to B and also whether they support a path from B to A. Checking both directions distinguishes support for the claimed order from support for the reverse order. If neither direction is established, the order remains underspecified on this representation.
Connect those checks to the three classification labels.

For an ordinary before-order claim, reachability in the claimed direction supports entailed; reachability in the reverse direction supports contradicted; and no established reachability in either direction supports undetermined. That is the intended three-way distinction, assuming the represented constraints yield a coherent interpretation. The proposal does not state a rule for resolving a case in which both directions are supported.
So checking both directions is important even if we mainly want to know whether the claim follows?

Yes. Failure to establish A before B does not by itself establish B before A. The reverse-direction check distinguishes a claim that conflicts with an established reverse ordering from a claim whose order is simply not determined. That is how the approach can preserve uncertainty instead of converting missing evidence into contradiction.
Suppose a correction changes one extracted constraint. Should every other extracted constraint be removed?

Not on the basis of this proposal. The provenance tags and incremental recomputation are meant to focus attention on constraints and consequences affected by the correction. A constraint supported by narrative information that the correction does not change should not be treated as changed merely because a correction occurred elsewhere. Whether a particular derived judgment is unaffected still depends on its actual support.
Would that directly address the requirement to preserve ≥95% of previously correct temporal judgments unaffected by corrections?

It is a proposed way to pursue that requirement: localize the consequences of a correction while retaining previously correct judgments that it does not affect. The ≥95% figure remains the preservation target, not a measured result of this proposal. The approach must also update affected judgments rather than preserving them indiscriminately.
And how does it relate to the macro-F1 ≥0.85 target?

The proposed classification mechanism aims to assign entailed, contradicted, or undetermined to temporal claims, the same three classes in the macro-F1 ≥0.85 requirement on unseen event structures. The proposal alone does not establish that score. In particular, its classifications depend on whether the extracted constraints adequately reflect what the narrative does and does not establish.
Does provenance itself make an extracted temporal constraint correct?

No. A provenance tag identifies the narrative basis attributed to a constraint; it is not proof that the extraction is accurate. The proposal distinguishes the source of a purported constraint from the later reasoning over constraints, but it does not claim to eliminate extraction errors.
I also don't want an unstated order introduced just to make the reachability check produce a definite answer.

That would run against the goal. Where the constraints do not establish either ordering, bidirectional reachability should leave the claim undetermined rather than filling the gap with an assumed order. The proposal is useful precisely because an absent path in the claimed direction and an established path in the reverse direction have different meanings.
Is it fair to say the correction affects provenance first, then the relevant inferred relationships, then the claim labels?

That captures the intended flow at a conceptual level: a correction prompts reconsideration of the constraints associated with the corrected narrative information; the affected temporal closure is recomputed; and claims are classified using reachability in both directions. It describes the proposal, not an implemented or validated sequence of operations.
And if a temporal claim stays supported by unchanged constraints, the correction alone shouldn't force its label to change?

Correct. A correction is a reason to reconsider what it affects, not a reason to overturn every existing judgment. Keeping unaffected, previously correct judgments while updating affected ones is the point of pairing provenance-tagged constraints with incremental recomputation.

The key question for me now is whether provenance-tagged closure updates can distinguish event orders that depend on a correction from pairs whose order is genuinely unspecified, without changing unrelated judgments.

That is the question to investigate, rather than a capability we can assume. The distinction is between an order whose support changes with corrected narrative information and a pair for which the narrative establishes no order in either direction. At the same time, a correction should not disturb judgments it leaves unaffected.
What makes an event order correction-dependent?

Its warranted conclusion depends on information that the correction changes. That dependence could be direct, through a temporal constraint associated with the corrected information, or indirect, through a consequence that relies on such a constraint. Simply mentioning an event in the correction would not, by itself, show that every judgment involving that event must change.
And what do you mean by genuinely unspecified, rather than merely not written as a direct statement?

An order can be implicit in a chain of temporal constraints even if no sentence states it directly. A genuinely unspecified pair is one for which the available narrative information does not establish either ordering, including through such consequences. The distinction matters because absence of a direct statement is not the same as absence of an inference.
Could you illustrate that distinction abstractly?

Suppose, just as an illustration, that the available constraints establish A before B and B before C. A before C follows even if it was never stated outright. If the narrative supplies no ordering path between C and D in either direction, their order remains unspecified on that information. These letters are only an illustration of the distinction, not a claim about any particular narrative.
How does provenance help when one of those links is corrected?

It identifies which extracted constraint is associated with the corrected information. That allows the proposed closure update to reconsider consequences supported by that constraint, rather than treating every inferred order as equally exposed to the correction. Whether it succeeds in separating affected from unaffected judgments is exactly what the question asks.
If the A-before-C conclusion depended on the corrected link, would we automatically reverse it?

No. Reconsidering its support is not the same as asserting the opposite. After the correction, the available constraints might support the same order through other information, support the reverse order, or leave the order undetermined. The conclusion should follow what the corrected narrative establishes, not an automatic reversal rule.
So a correction-dependent judgment might become undetermined?

Yes, conceptually. If the information supporting an order is changed and the resulting narrative establishes neither that order nor its reverse, the claim would be undetermined. The question is whether the proposed updates can recognize that outcome instead of preserving an inference that has lost its support or inventing a new definite order.
What is the corresponding risk for a genuinely unspecified pair?

The risk is assigning a definite order despite the corrected narrative still leaving the pair open. A closure update should not treat the mere arrival of a correction as evidence about every event pair. For a genuinely unspecified pair, neither direction is warranted by the available temporal information.
Where does bidirectional reachability enter this question?

It supplies the proposed way to distinguish the outcomes for a queried order. For a claim that A precedes B, support in that direction can warrant entailed, support in the reverse direction can warrant contradicted, and neither direction can warrant undetermined. After a correction, the question is whether the updated closure presents the right reachability relationships while leaving unrelated ones intact.
Does an absent path prove that the original narrative was genuinely silent?

Not necessarily. An absent path in the extracted constraints may reflect a genuinely underspecified narrative, but it could also reflect a constraint the LLM failed to extract. Provenance-tagged closure updates can only reason over the temporal information represented. That is one reason to frame the distinction as an open question rather than presume the method settles it.
What would count as an unrelated judgment in this discussion?

It is a judgment whose warranted status the correction does not affect. That is a matter of support, not simply whether the claim uses different event names from the corrected sentence. A correction can have indirect temporal consequences; conversely, mentioning an event does not necessarily change every order involving it.
Could an unaffected judgment still need to be checked during an update?

It might be considered while determining what the correction affects, but its warranted label should remain unchanged if its support is unaffected. The question is whether incremental recomputation can make that distinction reliably, rather than assuming that every considered judgment must change or that every old judgment must be retained.
I want to keep the two possible mistakes separate: changing an unrelated judgment, and failing to change a correction-dependent one.

They are distinct mistakes. The first introduces an unwarranted change where the narrative still supports the prior judgment. The second leaves an affected judgment in place despite a change to what supports it. A further concern is turning a genuinely unspecified order into a definite one. The question asks whether provenance-tagged closure updates can navigate all of those distinctions.
Would knowing the source of a constraint be enough to identify every judgment that depends on it?

Not by itself. Provenance associates a constraint with its narrative basis; determining which inferred orders rely on that constraint also requires accounting for how constraints contribute to closure. The proposal brings provenance and closure updates together, but the question remains whether their combination can separate correction-dependent orders from unspecified pairs without disturbing unrelated judgments.
So the issue is not just whether an update changes something, but whether it changes the right things and leaves unresolved orders unresolved?

Exactly. The inquiry concerns selectivity as well as correctness of the resulting temporal classifications: revise orders whose warrant changes, preserve unaffected judgments, and keep pairs undetermined when neither ordering follows. Nothing in the question establishes that the proposed approach already achieves that.
Can we state a testable hypothesis about provenance-scoped closure that addresses this question?

The hypothesis is that provenance-scoped closure will yield macro-F1 ≥0.85, undetermined-class F1 ≥0.85, and unaffected-judgment retention ≥95% on unseen event structures. These are predicted outcomes, not reported results.
Why include an undetermined-class target separately from macro-F1?

Macro-F1 averages performance across the entailed, contradicted, and undetermined classes. A macro-F1 of at least 0.85 would not, on its own, require undetermined-class F1 to reach 0.85. The separate threshold makes performance on unresolved temporal claims an explicit part of the hypothesis.
So both F1 thresholds are 0.85, but they refer to different quantities?

Yes. The hypothesis sets ≥0.85 for macro-F1 across the three temporal-claim classes and ≥0.85 specifically for the undetermined class. Meeting one threshold would not automatically establish that the other has been met.
What does undetermined-class F1 capture that a simple count of undetermined answers would not?

It concerns how well the undetermined label is assigned: whether genuinely unresolved claims receive it and whether claims whose order is established are incorrectly given it. A model could label many claims undetermined without distinguishing uncertainty well. The ≥0.85 undetermined-class F1 threshold is a prediction about classification performance, not about how often that label appears.
Does the hypothesis say that every unspecified pair must be classified correctly?

No. It states an undetermined-class F1 threshold of at least 0.85, not perfect classification of every pair. The underlying concern remains whether orders left unspecified by the narrative are kept distinct from orders affected by a correction.
Why is the retention threshold expressed separately from either F1 score?

Retention concerns stability under corrections: whether judgments unaffected by a correction keep their warranted status. The F1 thresholds concern temporal-claim classification. The hypothesis predicts both strong classification and ≥95% unaffected-judgment retention; a classification score alone would not state how well unrelated judgments are preserved across a correction.
What exactly does the ≥95% apply to?

It applies to unaffected-judgment retention on unseen event structures. In the context of the goal, the relevant judgments are previously correct temporal judgments that a narrative correction does not affect. The hypothesis predicts retaining at least 95% of those; it does not say to preserve a judgment whose support the correction changes.
If a judgment changes because the correction genuinely changes its support, does that count against unaffected-judgment retention?

No. Such a judgment is affected, so changing it is not a failure to retain an unaffected judgment. The retention figure must not be read as a reason to keep an answer that the corrected narrative no longer warrants.
Does ≥95% retention say how successfully affected judgments are updated?

Not by itself. It quantifies retention of unaffected judgments. The hypothesis also predicts classification performance, but it does not state a separate numerical target specifically for the fraction of affected judgments updated correctly. We should not turn the 95% figure into that different metric.
How does provenance-scoped closure relate to these predicted outcomes?

The hypothesis is that limiting closure updates according to provenance will help keep the effects of a correction focused on the inferences that depend on it. That could support retention of unaffected judgments while allowing the temporal classifications to reflect the corrected information. Whether it actually yields the stated F1 and retention thresholds remains to be established.
Is the idea that an absent temporal relationship should remain absent unless the corrected narrative supplies a reason to infer it?

Conceptually, yes. If neither ordering of a pair follows from the available temporal information, a correction elsewhere should not manufacture an ordering between them. The undetermined-class F1 threshold makes that aspect of the hypothesis visible rather than relying only on overall classification performance.
Would a strong undetermined-class F1 alone show that the system handles corrections selectively?

No. It would speak to classification of undetermined claims, but not by itself to preservation of unrelated judgments when a narrative is corrected. That is why the hypothesis also specifies ≥95% unaffected-judgment retention.
Likewise, could high retention coexist with poor treatment of unspecified pairs?

In principle, yes. Retaining unaffected judgments and identifying genuinely undetermined orders are different properties. The hypothesis sets thresholds for both, alongside macro-F1, rather than treating any one measure as a substitute for the others.
What does “on unseen event structures” qualify in the hypothesis?

It is the stated condition for the predicted outcomes: macro-F1 ≥0.85, undetermined-class F1 ≥0.85, and unaffected-judgment retention ≥95% are all hypothesized on unseen event structures. The node does not specify particular structures or how they would be selected.
Should I describe those numbers as expected measurements?

You can describe them as predicted thresholds in the hypothesis. Avoid presenting them as measurements already obtained: the hypothesis says provenance-scoped closure *will yield* those values, not that an evaluation has demonstrated them.
And if one threshold were met but another were not, would that satisfy this hypothesis as written?

No. As written, it predicts all three outcomes together. Meeting macro-F1 ≥0.85 without undetermined-class F1 ≥0.85, for example, would not meet the full prediction; nor would meeting both F1 thresholds while falling below ≥95% unaffected-judgment retention.
Does the hypothesis require perfect preservation of unrelated judgments?
No. Its retention threshold is ≥95%, not 100%. That numerical distinction matters even though preserving unrelated judgments is the motivating concern.
I want the wording to make clear that the method is proposed and these outcomes are uncertain.

Then frame it as a hypothesis: provenance-scoped closure is predicted to achieve macro-F1 ≥0.85, undetermined-class F1 ≥0.85, and unaffected-judgment retention ≥95% on unseen event structures. That states the method, each threshold, and the condition without implying the prediction has already been confirmed.
How should we test the extraction-and-closure approach rather than just discuss what it might do?

The planned activity is to test extraction-and-closure on TempoRev-500 graph-disjoint correction pairs with gold partial orders. The measurements are macro-F1, undetermined F1, retention, and update accuracy. That would examine both the temporal classifications and what happens to judgments when a narrative is corrected; it is a test to carry out, not a result already obtained.
What does “correction pairs” mean for this activity?

It indicates paired narrative conditions involving a correction, so temporal judgments can be considered in relation to the narrative before and after that correction. The activity does not specify the content of the pairs or a particular correction format.
Why does the description say graph-disjoint?

Graph-disjoint is a condition on the event structures used in the test: the relevant graphs are to be disjoint rather than reused as the same event structure. It matters to the stated interest in performance on unseen structures. The node does not spell out a partitioning procedure or how graph disjointness is enforced.
Should we infer from the name TempoRev-500 that there are exactly 500 pairs?
No. TempoRev-500 is the specified name of the test set. The activity does not separately state a pair count, so I would preserve the name without inferring the number of correction pairs from it.
What role do the gold partial orders play?

They provide a reference for the temporal ordering that the activity is meant to assess. A partial order can establish some relationships while leaving others unspecified, which is important for distinguishing an order that follows from one that the narrative does not settle. Calling them gold partial orders identifies their reference role; it does not imply that every pair of events has a specified order.
If two events have no direct relation in a gold partial order, are they automatically an undetermined pair?

Not solely because no direct relation is listed. An ordering may follow through other established relationships in the partial order. The relevant distinction is whether the gold ordering establishes either direction, directly or through its consequences. If neither direction follows, the pair can remain undetermined.
How does this test both extraction and closure?

The activity tests the extraction-and-closure approach as a whole: temporal information has to be extracted from the narratives, and the resulting constraints and their consequences have to support the claim classifications and correction updates. The activity does not state separate extraction-only and closure-only measurements, so the listed metrics should not be presented as isolating those stages.
Remind me what macro-F1 measures in this context.

It summarizes classification performance across the temporal-claim labels—entailed, contradicted, and undetermined—by averaging their F1 scores with equal weight. In this activity, macro-F1 is one of the measurements to take on the specified correction pairs. No measured macro-F1 is supplied here.
Why also measure undetermined F1?

Because the ability to leave genuinely unspecified event orders unresolved deserves direct attention. Macro-F1 covers all three labels, whereas undetermined F1 focuses on how well the undetermined label is assigned. Reporting both would keep that aspect visible rather than relying on the aggregate alone.
Could a system get a reasonable macro-F1 while guessing orders for some unspecified pairs?

Conceptually, yes. A summary across labels does not tell us by itself how every undetermined claim was handled. Measuring undetermined F1 separately helps show whether the approach distinguishes unresolved orders from entailed or contradicted ones. The activity does not state what the resulting scores will be.
What would retention tell us?

Retention concerns whether temporal judgments that a correction does not affect remain intact. It addresses the risk of changing unrelated judgments simply because the narrative was corrected. Here it is a measurement to take, not a reported level of stability.
Does retention include keeping a judgment that the correction makes wrong?
No. Retention is about unaffected judgments. A judgment whose warrant changes with the correction needs to be assessed as an update, not counted as something to keep merely for the sake of stability.
Then what is update accuracy meant to capture?

It concerns whether judgments affected by corrections are updated correctly under the gold temporal ordering. It complements retention: one measure concerns not disturbing what is unaffected, while the other concerns getting the changed judgments right. The activity names update accuracy but does not specify a detailed calculation for it.
Could high retention alone make the test look successful if the approach never changes an answer?

That is why measuring update accuracy as well matters. An approach that leaves every answer untouched might retain unaffected judgments yet fail on judgments that should change. Considering both measurements keeps stability distinct from responsiveness to corrections.
And could high update accuracy hide a problem with unrelated judgments?

Yes, considered on its own, update accuracy would not describe how often unaffected judgments were disturbed. Measuring retention alongside it addresses that separate concern. Neither number should be used as a stand-in for the other.
Do the gold partial orders help evaluate both kinds of judgment?

They provide the reference ordering against which temporal claims can be assessed in the paired narratives. That supports examining classifications and whether judgments after a correction align with the applicable order. Identifying which judgments are affected and unaffected remains part of interpreting the correction pairs; the activity does not give a more detailed labeling procedure.
I don't want to imply that a partial order supplies a definite answer for every before-or-after question.

It does not. A partial order permits unresolved relationships. If neither direction between two events follows from the reference order, treating that pair as definitely ordered would lose the uncertainty the test is meant to examine. This is one reason undetermined F1 belongs among the measurements.
Is “contradicted” the same as “not present in the gold partial order”?

No. For a claim that one event precedes another, an established reverse order can contradict it. Merely lacking support for the claimed direction does not establish the reverse; the claim may instead be undetermined. Consequences of the partial order must be considered, not just whether a direct link is written down.
Does this activity already tell us whether extraction errors or closure errors are responsible for a wrong classification?

No. It calls for testing extraction-and-closure and measuring four outcomes, but it does not prescribe an error-attribution analysis. A wrong classification could raise questions about either part of the approach; the listed measurements alone do not assign a cause.
Are any metric values given for TempoRev-500 here?

No. The activity specifies where to test—the TempoRev-500 graph-disjoint correction pairs with gold partial orders—and what to measure: macro-F1, undetermined F1, retention, and update accuracy. It supplies no observed scores or outcome for the test.
So even though this activity is intended to evaluate the hypothesis, we should describe it as a planned test?

Yes. “Test extraction-and-closure” states the activity, not that the test has already been completed or has supported the hypothesis. The four named measurements would provide distinct views of classification, handling of unspecified orders, preservation of unaffected judgments, and correctness of updates.
What results did closure achieve on TempoRev-500?

On TempoRev-500, closure achieved 0.88 macro-F1, 0.86 undetermined F1, 97% unaffected-judgment retention, and 90% corrected-claim update accuracy. Those are the reported measurements for this evaluation.
Can you separate what each number tells us?

The 0.88 macro-F1 summarizes classification across entailed, contradicted, and undetermined temporal claims. The 0.86 undetermined F1 focuses specifically on the undetermined class. The 97% retention concerns judgments unaffected by a correction, while the 90% update accuracy concerns corrected claims that do call for an update. They describe related but different aspects of performance.
Is 0.88 macro-F1 an accuracy percentage?
No. Macro-F1 is an average of the class-level F1 scores, with each class receiving equal weight. The reported value is 0.88; it should not be relabeled as 88% classification accuracy.
Why report undetermined F1 when macro-F1 already includes that class?

Reporting 0.86 undetermined F1 makes performance on claims with unresolved event order visible on its own. Macro-F1 includes that class in an average, but the average alone does not tell us its individual score.
Does 0.86 undetermined F1 mean every genuinely unspecified pair was left unresolved?

No. An F1 of 0.86 is not perfect performance. It summarizes how the undetermined class was handled, but it does not say that every unspecified pair received the right label or identify particular errors.
How should I read the 97% figure?

It is the reported unaffected-judgment retention: 97% of judgments in the unaffected category were retained. It speaks to stability where a correction should not change the judgment, not to whether judgments affected by the correction were updated correctly.
So the 90% figure covers the other concern?

Yes. The reported 90% corrected-claim update accuracy addresses correctness on claims that call for updating after a correction. It complements the retention measurement: one concerns keeping unaffected judgments intact, and the other concerns getting corrected claims right.
Can I infer that the remaining 10% of corrected claims were all left unchanged?
No. The reported update accuracy does not break down the errors. An incorrect update could take more than one form, and these results do not say which occurred.
Likewise, do we know what happened to the judgments outside the retained 97%?
Not from these four figures. The retention number tells us the reported rate for unaffected judgments, but it does not provide individual cases or explain the judgments that were not retained.
Could I combine 97% retention and 90% update accuracy into one overall correction score?

Not from the information given. They apply to different categories of judgments, and no combined score or weighting between those categories is reported. Keeping them separate preserves what each measurement actually describes.
Do these results tell us whether the LLM's extraction or the closure step caused any particular error?

No. The figures report outcomes for closure on TempoRev-500, including classification and correction behavior. They do not attribute individual mistakes to extraction, closure computation, or another part of the approach.
What can we say about uncertainty from these measurements without overreaching?

We can say that undetermined F1 was 0.86 on TempoRev-500, giving a specific measurement for the undetermined class. We cannot conclude from that number that every underspecified order was preserved as uncertain, or describe which event pairs were mislabeled.
And what can we say about selective updating?

The reported figures distinguish the two sides of selective updating: 97% unaffected-judgment retention and 90% corrected-claim update accuracy. That distinction matters because preserving an unaffected judgment and correctly changing a corrected claim are not the same operation. The aggregate figures do not show how any particular correction played out.
Should the numbers be described as predictions or observations?

As reported observations from TempoRev-500: closure achieved 0.88 macro-F1, 0.86 undetermined F1, 97% unaffected-judgment retention, and 90% corrected-claim update accuracy. The evidence states those measured outcomes, not merely expected values.
Do we have a comparison against another approach?
No comparison score is provided in this evidence. These four numbers describe closure's reported performance on TempoRev-500; they do not by themselves establish an advantage over another approach.
Does the evidence give the number of claims or a confidence interval?
No. It reports the four metric values, but not the number of evaluated claims, an uncertainty interval, or a breakdown by type of correction. We should leave those details unspecified.

Keep versioned SAT for uncertainty audits, with its 0.91 undetermined F1 and 98% unaffected-judgment retention. Prefer the hybrid on macro-F1, retain contrastive fine-tuning as an alternative, and defer retrieval. Those are distinct parts of the decision rather than a choice to use one approach for every purpose.
What makes versioned SAT useful specifically for uncertainty audits?

Its temporal-constraint model allows a claim and its opposite to be checked against the applicable narrative version. If both remain possible, the claim should not be presented as a settled order. The decision keeps SAT in that auditing role, supported by the stated 0.91 undetermined F1; it does not claim that every uncertain pair is identified perfectly.
Does 0.91 undetermined F1 mean that 91% of event pairs are unordered?

No. It is an F1 score for classifying the undetermined category, not the proportion of event pairs whose order is unspecified. It also does not guarantee that every individual undetermined claim was labeled correctly.
What does the 98% figure cover?

It is unaffected-judgment retention: the rate at which previously correct temporal judgments unaffected by corrections remain intact. It is not an update-accuracy score, and it does not call for preserving a judgment whose warrant a correction changes.
Could an undetermined judgment be among those retained?

Yes. If a correction still leaves a pair’s order open, its previously correct undetermined judgment can be unaffected and remain in place. If the correction establishes an order, that judgment needs reconsideration instead.
If SAT has those strengths, why prefer the hybrid?

The preference stated here is specifically for the hybrid’s macro-F1. Keeping SAT for uncertainty audits and preferring the hybrid on that classification measure can coexist; neither statement says one approach dominates every measure or every setting.
Is the hybrid being preferred on undetermined F1 and retention too?

That is not what this decision says. It assigns versioned SAT an uncertainty-audit role, explicitly noting 0.91 undetermined F1 and 98% retention, while expressing a preference for the hybrid’s macro-F1. Extending that preference to the other two measures would change its scope.
What does macro-F1 represent in that preference?

Macro-F1 averages F1 across the entailed, contradicted, and undetermined temporal-claim classes with equal weight. Preferring the hybrid’s macro-F1 is a preference about that aggregate classification measure, not a statement that every claim or every individual class is handled better by the hybrid.
Are we selecting SAT to replace the hybrid for all decisions involving corrections?
No. The decision keeps versioned SAT for uncertainty audits and prefers the hybrid’s macro-F1. It does not say that SAT replaces the hybrid as the general classification approach.
Could an audit flag an unsupported definite order without itself deciding which approach to deploy?

Conceptually, yes. An uncertainty audit asks whether the applicable temporal constraints warrant a definite judgment or leave alternatives possible. The decision to keep SAT for that purpose is separate from preferring the hybrid on macro-F1. It does not specify an operational procedure for feeding audit findings into another approach.
When both orders remain possible in a SAT audit, is one of them entailed because it is satisfiable?

No. Satisfiable means possible. If the claim and its alternative are both compatible with the applicable constraints, the order is not settled by those constraints. Treating one possible order as entailed would erase the uncertainty the audit is meant to examine.
And if a correction removes support for one order, do we automatically assert the reverse?

No. The applicable constraints might still support the original order through another route, establish the reverse, or leave the pair undetermined. Neither versioned SAT’s auditing role nor the hybrid preference changes that distinction.
Where does contrastive fine-tuning fit in the decision?

Retain it as an alternative. That preserves a training-based option without declaring it the preferred method on macro-F1, assigning it the SAT uncertainty-audit role, or claiming it must be deployed alongside the hybrid.
Does retaining an alternative imply that its predictions are always consistent with the hybrid or SAT?

No. The decision says nothing about agreement on individual claims or how to resolve disagreements. Calling contrastive fine-tuning an alternative keeps that option available without inventing a combination rule.
What does “defer retrieval” mean here?

It means not proceeding with retrieval as the selected approach at this point. Deferral is not a claim that retrieval can never be useful, and this decision does not specify a condition or timetable for reconsidering it.
Should I describe retrieval as disproved or unusable in every temporal setting?

No. The decision is to defer retrieval, not to make a universal judgment about every retrieval-based temporal system or every event structure. Its other parts—SAT for audits, hybrid macro-F1 preference, and the contrastive alternative—should likewise retain their stated scope.
Could we phrase this as four different roles rather than rank every method from best to worst?

Yes. Versioned SAT is kept for uncertainty audits; the hybrid is preferred on macro-F1; contrastive fine-tuning remains an alternative; retrieval is deferred. That expresses the decisions without inventing a complete ranking across all measures.
Is 98% retention the same as saying all unrelated judgments were preserved?
No. It is 98%, not 100%. It supports keeping versioned SAT for the stated purpose but does not claim perfect retention of every unaffected judgment.
Do these SAT numbers tell us how accurately it updated claims affected by corrections?

No separate affected-update accuracy is specified in this decision. The SAT figures here are 0.91 undetermined F1 and 98% unaffected-judgment retention. Neither should be relabeled as an affected-update score.
Should the preference for hybrid macro-F1 be read as a promise that it will be highest on every new event topology?

No. The decision states a macro-F1 preference; it does not guarantee a result on every future topology or assert superiority on all temporal-judgment measures. The distinction between a stated preference and an unrestricted performance guarantee matters.
What if an event pair has no direct ordering statement but is ordered through intermediate events? Would the uncertainty-audit role call it undetermined?

Not just because a direct statement is missing. Applicable constraints may imply an order through intermediate events. The audit should preserve uncertainty when the information does not settle the claim, not when an order is merely indirect.
Can you give me the decision in one sentence while keeping the measures attached to the right approach?

Keep versioned SAT for uncertainty audits, noting its 0.91 undetermined F1 and 98% unaffected-judgment retention; prefer the hybrid’s macro-F1, retain contrastive fine-tuning as an alternative, and defer retrieval.
